newsitem.title: UK: Euro products outlook-heating oil, naphtha to gain.
newsitem.headline: Euro products outlook-heating oil, naphtha to gain.

text.p: Heating oil and naphtha look set to lead the European oil products market this week, but gasoline and fuel oil have less upward potential, said oil traders.
Gas oil is expected to split into a two-tier market with the premium for low 0.05 percent sulphur diesel over 0.2 percent sulphur heating oil coming under pressure, traders said.
Dealers said an unusually large 400,000 to 800,000 tonnes of 0.2 percent product will be needed for delivery into the Nov IPE futures contract on its Tuesday expiry.
IPE brokers speculated that the Nov supply squeeze, which widened the backwardation over Dec by $5 to $8.50 a tonne last week, was caused by a head-to-head between two trading houses.
One has established a large long position, betting that the other, with a large short position, will not be able to deliver its commitments and so buy back its position at a higher price.
The result will be a further leap in the front month spread and stronger physical prices, traders said.
In contrast, premiums for 0.05 percent sulphur diesel barges over benchmark futures, which have already slid some $25 since mid-October are expected to dip below the $10 a tonne mark.
"When premiums were as far out as $35 refiners maximised output...now the demand just isn't there." said one trader.
Naphtha is set to rise on the back of strong buying in Nov swaps, although fundamentals remain balanced.
Cargoes are set to edge up from near $220 cif while Nov swaps were likely to move from just under $220 to the mid-$220s, said traders, and widen the backwardation to December from the current $8.
Heavy long positions in Nov swaps will create upwards pressure but fundamentals are neutral, with the arbitrage to the U.S. shut and very weak petrochemical demand.
Traders said gasoline will continue to come under pressure, but buying ahead of the U.K. budget on Nov 26, witnessed last week, should cushion any falls.
Eurograde barges, which slipped from highs last week near $230 toward a low near $217, could drop to $200, traders said.
The price outlook for heavy fuel is also uncertain.

The recent overhang of Russian straight run fuel oil on the cracked market is expected to ease, which should allow cracked prices to rise slightly. "The big overhang has been thinned and it looks like gradually drying up," said one trader.
But gains will be modest with supply-demand mostly balanced.
Prices in Rotterdam could move up to the mid teens, but probably no higher. High sulphur cracked fuel in the Mediterranean is set steady, with a 50,000 tonne Syrian cargo likely to limit gains.

The soggy low sulphur cracked sector will look to Enel, the Italian state power company, for support, but some traders feel last week's late push may falter if physical demand doesn't kick in. A late paper deal at $125 late Friday may not be to carry through. "I see $135 cif as a ceiling," said one dealer.
